citation.title: Conservative Variance Estimation for Sampling Designs with Zero Pairwise Inclusion Probabilities

standing_assumptions:
The work is a short theory paper (Survey Methodology, June 2013, Vol. 39, No. 1, printed pp. 231–241; the article is PDF pp. 3–13 of the staged main.pdf) with two propositions and three corollaries, each with a printed proof, and an official simulation supplement (staged/supplements/smj_suppl.pdf, printed pp. A1–A10) that the article points to on p. 239. Everything below was read from the rendered page images (the staged pages, and the staged PDFs re-rendered at 220 dpi when this list was fixed).
[Population and design: Section 2, first paragraph, pp. 232–233 (PDF pp. 4–5)] “Consider a population $U$ indexed by $1, \ldots, k, \ldots N$ and a sampling design such that the probability of inclusion in the sample for unit $k$ is $\pi_k$, and the joint inclusion probability for units $k$ and $l$ is $\pi_{kl}$. Under a measurable design, there are two conditions: (1) $\pi_k > 0$ and $\pi_k$ is known for all $k \in U$ and (2) $\pi_{kl} > 0$ and $\pi_{kl}$ is known for all $k, l \in U$. Non-measurable designs include those for which either of the two conditions for a measurable design do not hold. Failure to meet the former condition precludes unbiased estimation of totals.”
[Estimator of the total and inclusion indicators: p. 233 (PDF p. 5)] “The Horvitz-Thompson estimator of a population total is $\hat t = \sum_{k \in s} y_k/\pi_k = \sum_{k \in U} I_k\, y_k/\pi_k$, where $I_k \in \{0, 1\}$ is unit $k$'s inclusion indicator, the only stochastic component of the expression, with $\mathrm{E}(I_k) = \pi_k$, the inclusion probability, and $s$ and $U$ refer to the sample and the population, respectively. Define $\mathrm{E}(I_k I_l) = \pi_{kl}$, which is the probability that both units $k$ and $l$ from $U$ are included in the sample. Since $I_k I_k = I_k$, $\mathrm{E}(I_k I_k) = \pi_{kk} = \pi_k$ by construction. When condition 1 holds, as we assume throughout, the Horvitz-Thompson estimator is unbiased.”
[Variance and its estimator under measurability: Section 2.1, p. 233 (PDF p. 5)] “By Horvitz and Thompson (1952), the variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator for the total is $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat t) = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in U}\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l} = \sum_{k \in U}\mathrm{Var}(I_k)\left(\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\right)^2 + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in U\backslash k}\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}.$$ We label a sample from a measurable design, $s^M$, and an unbiased estimator for $\mathrm{Var}(\hat t)$ on $s^M$ is $$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t) = \sum_{k \in s^M}\sum_{l \in s^M}\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l} = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in U} I_k I_l\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l},$$ where the only stochastic part of the expression is $I_k I_l$, and unbiasedness is by $\mathrm{E}(I_k I_l) = \pi_{kl}$.”
[Non-measurable designs, the term $A$ and the sample $s^0$: Section 2.2, pp. 233–234 (PDF pp. 5–6)] “We now examine the case where condition 2 does not hold: $\pi_{kl} = 0$ for some units $k, l \in U$. Because $I_k$ is a Bernoulli random variable with probability $\pi_k$, $\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l) = \pi_{kl} - \pi_k\pi_l$ for $k \ne l$, and $\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_k) = \mathrm{Var}(I_k) = \pi_k(1 - \pi_k)$. Then, we can re-express the variance above as, $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat t) = \sum_{k \in U}\pi_k(1 - \pi_k)\left(\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\right)^2 + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in U\backslash k}(\pi_{kl} - \pi_k\pi_l)\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}$$ $$= \sum_{k \in U}\pi_k(1 - \pi_k)\left(\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\right)^2 + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} > 0\}}(\pi_{kl} - \pi_k\pi_l)\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l} - \underbrace{\sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}} y_k y_l}_{A}.$$ For $k$ and $l$ such that $\pi_{kl} = 0$, the sampling design will never permit unbiased estimation of the component of the variance labeled as $A$ above, since we will never observe $y_k$ and $y_l$ together. We label a sample from a design where condition 2 fails as $s^0$. When $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$ is applied to $s^0$, the result is unbiased for $\mathrm{Var}(\hat t) + A$.” On the page the underbrace spans the double sum $\sum_k\sum_l y_k y_l$ only, not the minus sign before it, so $A = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}} y_k y_l$; Proposition 1 (p. 234) and the display of $A$ at the head of p. 239 (PDF p. 11) agree with this.
[Conventions that every statement inherits] The outcomes $y_1, \ldots, y_N$ are fixed real numbers; expectation, variance and covariance are over the sampling design alone (‘the only stochastic component’ is $I_k$). Condition 1 ($\pi_k > 0$ for every $k$) is assumed throughout; ‘known’ plays no part in any mathematical statement. A double sum $\sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}}$ runs over ordered pairs $(k, l)$ of distinct units with $\pi_{kl} = 0$, so each unordered pair is counted twice; $\sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U:\pi_{kl} > 0\}}$ includes the diagonal $l = k$ (as $\pi_{kk} = \pi_k > 0$). On a sample $s^0$ the estimator $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$ is the sum over pairs of sampled units, which the proof of Proposition 1 (p. 234) writes as $\sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U:\pi_{kl} > 0\}} I_k I_l\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}$.
[What the paper does not print] No probability space is displayed: a sampling design is a probability distribution on the subsets $s \subseteq U$, with $I_k = 1$ exactly when $k \in s$. The paper does not say that $U$ is finite and non-empty other than through the indexing $1, \ldots, N$. In Section 3 the exponents $a_{kl}, b_{kl}$ are indexed by ordered pairs and are not required to be symmetric in $(k, l)$; $1/a_{kl} + 1/b_{kl} = 1$ with both positive forces $a_{kl}, b_{kl} > 1$; $|y|^{a}$ is the real power of a nonnegative number (so $|0|^{a} = 0$).
[Supplement, Section A, p. A1 (supplement PDF p. 1)] “In the simulations, expected values of $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)$ were computed exactly using expressions from Propositions 1 and 2 in the main text. Expected values for alternative estimators were computed using exact expressions for bias when available and via simulated sample draws otherwise. All simulations study expected values of estimators for the sampling variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator for the population mean, $$\hat\mu_{HT} \equiv \frac{1}{N}\hat t.$$” So in the supplement the estimand is $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_{HT}) = \mathrm{Var}(\hat t)/N^2$ and the estimators are $(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$ and $(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)$; by Proposition 1 the bias of $(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$ is $A/N^2$.
[Supplement, Section B, one unit per stratum: pp. A1–A2 (supplement PDF pp. 1–2)] “Simplifying that context, we consider two strata each of size $M$, in which case $N = 2M$. From each stratum a single unit is randomly sampled. Thus, for unit $k$ in stratum $s$, $$\pi_{ks} = \pi = \frac{1}{M},$$ and for units $k$ and $l$ in strata 1 or 2, we have $$\pi_{ks,lt} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } s = t \\ \frac{1}{M^2} & \text{if } s \neq t \end{cases}.$$ In stratum $s$, outcomes $y_s = (y_{1s}, ..., y_{Ms})$ are drawn as, $$y_{ks} = \alpha_s + \epsilon_{is},$$ where $\alpha_s$ is a stratum-specific constant and $\epsilon_{ks} \sim \mathrm{N}(0, 1)$. For the two strata, 1 and 2, we keep things simple by setting $\alpha_1 = \alpha = -\alpha_2$, in which case the intra-class correlation over strata is given by, $$\rho_{ICC} = \frac{\alpha^2}{\alpha^2 + 1/2}.$$ We simulated 1,000 sets of outcomes, $(y_1, y_2)$ over varying values of $M$ and $\rho_{ICC}$. To each set, we applied the single-unit-per-stratum design. Then, we computed three approximations of the sampling variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator of the population mean: 1. The Horvitz-Thompson estimator for the sampling variance of the estimator for the population mean, $(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$. 2. The bias-adjusted estimator, $(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)$. 3. The “collapsed stratum” estimator (Wolter, 2007, 51-2), which for this case, given unit $k$ from stratum 1 and unit $l$ from stratum 2 selected into $s^0$, equals, $$\widehat V_{CS}(\hat\mu_{HT}) = \frac{1}{N^2}\left(\frac{y_{k1}}{\pi_1} - \frac{y_{l2}}{\pi_2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}(y_{k1} - y_{l2})^2.$$” (The two misprints in these displays, the missing restriction to distinct units and $\epsilon_{is}$ for $\epsilon_{ks}$, are finding P027-E006; see P027-T18.) The supplement does not say that the errors $\epsilon_{ks}$ are independent, or that the two strata are sampled independently; both are the ordinary reading and are used by the validators.
[Supplement, Section C, systematic PPS sampling: pp. A3–A4 (supplement PDF pp. 3–4)] “For the simulations, a size variable, $x = (x_1, ..., x_N)$, is produced as a vector of $N$ random draws from a negative binomial distribution with mean 6, variance 16, and offset of 1 to avoid zero values. These settings were meant to recreate a data scenario roughly comparable to Wolter (2007, Ch. 8). An outcome variable, $y$, is created as, $$y_k = \beta x_k + \epsilon_k,$$ for $k = 1, ..., N$, where $\beta = \rho(\sigma_y/\sigma_x)$, $\epsilon_k$ is Gaussian noise with mean zero and standard deviation $\sigma_y\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}$, and $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_y$ are the standard deviation of the $N$ values in $x$ and $y$ respectively, where $\mathrm{E}_x(\sigma_x) = 4$ and we fix $\sigma_y = 30$ (again, to mimic data distributed as in Wolter (2007, Ch. 8)). Thus, $x$ and $y$ have a linear relationship through the origin and their correlation is given by $\rho$. Systematic PPS sampling was implemented such that each unit's first order inclusion probability is given by, $$\pi_k = \frac{x_k}{\sum_{l=1}^{N} x_l}m,$$ where $m$ is the size of the systematic sample, and joint inclusion probabilities are computed as per Madow (1949).” The with-replacement estimator (p. A3): $$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{WR}(\hat\mu_{HT}) = \frac{1}{N^2 m(m - 1)}\sum_{k \in s^0}\left(\frac{y_k}{p_k} - \hat t\right)^2,$$ “where $p_k = \pi_k/m$ is the notional “per-draw” selection probability.” The periodic design (pp. A3–A4): “we performed a second set of simulations where the size variable, $x$, was drawn as an $N$-length vector of repeating 2's and 10's, thus maintaining variance values that are comparable to the previous simulation. Also, so that we could provide an illustration of the performance of $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)$, we produced $y_k$ values in the same manner as above, but then worked with the demeaned value, $$\tilde y_k \equiv y_k - \bar y,$$ as the variable with which $\hat\mu_{HT}$ was computed.” The supplement does not display the systematic selection rule; the validators and the targets below use the usual cumulative-size rule with one uniform random start (unit $k$ occupies the interval $[c_{k-1}, c_k)$ with $c_k = \sum_{a \le k} x_a$; with $I = \sum_l x_l/m$ and $u$ uniform on $[0, I)$ the sample is the set of units whose intervals contain $u, u + I, \ldots, u + (m-1)I$), and the order $x = (2, 10, 2, 10, \ldots)$. The $(N, m)$ pairs of Tables A2 and A3 (pp. A7–A8) are $(8, 2), (40, 2), (120, 30), (600, 30), (240, 60), (1200, 60)$, so $q = N/m \in \{4, 20\}$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Table A3, rows 30, 40, 50, 60 (the $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{HT}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}$ means at $\rho = 0.99$, $N \ge 120$), with Section A's statement that these expected values ‘were computed exactly using expressions from Propositions 1 and 2’: the formal content of the finding (exact expectations in the stated design, their model moments, and a signal-free contrast); no corrected table values are available
canonical_claim.location: Supplement p. A8 (staged/supplements/smj_suppl.pdf, PDF p. 8), Table A3, rows 30, 40, 50, 60; supplement p. A1 (PDF p. 1), Section A, second sentence; the design on supplement pp. A3–A4 (PDF pp. 3–4)
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P027-N004, smallest_repair), verbatim: "For the described simulation, regenerate the affected Table A3 and Figure A3 quantities from the original populations using exact periodic phase probabilities, state the number of outcome populations and uncertainty, and revise the A4 cancellation explanation. In the stated model the HT negative bias is about 13.89% at sampling fraction 1/4 and 2.78% at fraction 1/20 in the ratio of model means. If the actual implementation differs, correct and validate the description instead. No exact replacement for the unknown realized rows is supplied."
As printed, Table A3 (supplement p. A8), rows (row; $N$; $m$; $\rho$; True Var; mean $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{HT}$; mean $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}$; mean $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{WR}$; relative bias of $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{HT}$, $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}$): 30; 120; 30; 0.99; 1578.87; 1412.15; 2029.28; 1.07; -0.11, 0.29. 40; 600; 30; 0.99; 1587.01; 1564.34; 2396.58; 1.08; -0.01, 0.51. 50; 240; 60; 0.99; 1581.13; 1430.59; 2032.07; 0.52; -0.10, 0.29. 60; 1200; 60; 0.99; 1586.32; 1562.38; 2395.86; 0.53; -0.02, 0.51.
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis (validator's derivation.md, sections 1–5).
Setting. The periodic design of P027-T2: $N = mq$, $q$ a positive even integer, $m \ge 2$, sizes $x_k = 2$ ($k$ odd), $10$ ($k$ even), possible samples $G_g$ with probabilities $p_g = 1/(3q)$ ($g$ odd), $5/(3q)$ ($g$ even); $z$ any real vector with $\sum_i z_i = 0$; $Y_g = \sum_{i \in G_g} z_i$; $Q = \sum_i z_i^2$. All four quantities below are on the population-mean scale: $V = \mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_{HT})$; $H = \mathrm{E}[(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)]$; $C = \mathrm{E}[(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)]$ for the estimator applied to the original units; $W = \mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{WR}(\hat\mu_{HT})]$.
(i) [Exact design expectations, for every demeaned population.] $$V = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_g\frac{Y_g^2}{p_g}, \qquad H = V - B \ \text{ with } \ B = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_g Y_g^2 \ge 0, \qquad C - H = \frac{(N - m)Q}{N^2},$$ $$W = \frac{m\sum_g\big(\sum_{i \in G_g} z_i^2\big)/p_g - N^2 V}{N^2(m - 1)}.$$
(ii) [Model moments, second moments only.] The relative-bias quotients below are asserted only when $\mathrm E(V)>0$; the other moment identities retain the zero-variance case. Let $z_i = \beta(x_i - 6) + \epsilon_i - \bar\epsilon$ with $\beta$ constant and errors $\epsilon_i$ with mean zero, common variance $\sigma^2$ and zero covariances. Then $\mathrm{E}(Y_g^2) = 16m^2\beta^2 + \sigma^2(m - m^2/N)$ for every $g$, and $$\mathrm{E}(B) = \frac{16\beta^2}{q} + \frac{\sigma^2(N - m)}{N^2}, \quad \mathrm{E}(V) = \frac{9q}{5}\mathrm{E}(B), \quad \mathrm{E}(H) = \mathrm{E}(V) - \mathrm{E}(B), \quad \frac{\mathrm{E}(H) - \mathrm{E}(V)}{\mathrm{E}(V)} = -\frac{5}{9q},$$ $$\mathrm{E}(Q) = 16N\beta^2 + (N - 1)\sigma^2, \quad \mathrm{E}(C) = \mathrm{E}(H) + \frac{N - m}{N^2}\mathrm{E}(Q), \quad \mathrm{E}(W) = \frac{9}{5}\cdot\frac{\sigma^2}{m}.$$ With the supplement's calibration $\sigma^2 = 900(1 - \rho^2)$ and $\beta^2 = 900\rho^2(N - 1)/(16N)$ (so $\mathrm{E}(Q) = 900(N - 1)$), the values at $\rho = 0.99$ are, for $(N, m) = (120, 30)$: $\mathrm{E}(V) = 1575.3366$, $\mathrm{E}(H) = 1356.53985$, $\mathrm{E}(C) = 2025.91485$, $\mathrm{E}(W) = 1.0746$; for $(600, 30)$: $1586.1366$, $1542.07725$, $2395.65225$, $1.0746$; for $(240, 60)$: $1581.5493$, $1361.889675$, $2034.077175$, $0.5373$; for $(1200, 60)$: $1586.9493$, $1542.867375$, $2397.154875$, $0.5373$. The model relative bias of the uncorrected estimator is $-5/36 \approx -13.89\%$ at $q = 4$ and $-1/36 \approx -2.78\%$ at $q = 20$, against the printed $-0.11$, $-0.01$, $-0.10$, $-0.02$.
(iii) [A contrast in which the signal cancels exactly.] Put $R = \frac{5(q - 1)}{9q - 5}$, $c = \frac{6q}{9q - 5}$ and $T(z) = C - (1 + R)H$. The space of demeaned vectors is the orthogonal direct sum of: $\mathcal W$, the vectors that sum to zero within every $G_g$ (dimension $N - q$); $\mathcal P$, the multiples of $x - 6$ (dimension 1); $\mathcal L$, the vectors that are constant on each $G_g$, vanish on the $G_g$ with $g$ even, and sum to zero (dimension $d = q/2 - 1$); $\mathcal G$, the same with $g$ odd in place of $g$ even (dimension $d$). Writing $z = z_{\mathcal W} + z_{\mathcal P} + z_{\mathcal L} + z_{\mathcal G}$, $$T(z) = \frac{N - m}{N^2}\Big(\|z_{\mathcal W}\|^2 + c\,\|z_{\mathcal G}\|^2 - c\,\|z_{\mathcal L}\|^2\Big).$$ In particular $T(\beta(x - 6) + \eta) = T(\eta)$ for every real $\beta$ and every demeaned $\eta$ (the contrast does not depend on $\beta$ or on any signal-noise cross term), and $T(z) \ge -\frac{(N - m)c}{N^2}\|z_{\mathcal L}\|^2$.
(iv) [Gaussian noise.] If $\sigma^2>0$ and the $\epsilon_i$ are independent $\mathrm{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, then $T = a\,[X_{\mathcal W} + c\,(X_{\mathcal G} - X_{\mathcal L})]$ almost surely, with $a = (N - m)\sigma^2/N^2$ and $X_{\mathcal W}, X_{\mathcal G}, X_{\mathcal L}$ independent chi-squared variables with $N - q$, $d$ and $d$ degrees of freedom; $\mathrm{E}(T) = a(N - q) > 0$.
(v) [Tail bound.] For $\sigma^2>0$, let $\bar T$ be the average of $T$ over $K \ge 1$ generated populations, each with the noise law of (iv) (no independence across populations is needed), and let $k = ac$. For every $\ell > 0$, $$\Pr(\bar T \le -\ell) \le e^{-\ell/(4k)}\,2^{d/2} \le 2^{-(J - h)} \quad\text{whenever } J := \lfloor \ell/(4k)\rfloor > h := \lceil d/2\rceil.$$ (It uses $\bar T \ge -k\,\bar X_{\mathcal L}$, $\mathrm{E}[e^{X/4}] = 2^{f/2}$ for a chi-squared variable with $f$ degrees of freedom, convexity, and Markov's inequality.)
(vi) [The four rows.] From the printed means, $T_{\text{printed}} = C - (1 + R)H$ equals $-102561/1550 \approx -66.17$ (row 30; $R = 15/31$), $-29703/1750 \approx -16.97$ (row 40; $R = 19/35$), $-281297/3100 \approx -90.74$ (row 50) and $-25671/1750 \approx -14.67$ (row 60). If each printed mean is within $0.005$ of the average it reports, the average $\bar T$ is at most $-\ell$ with $\ell = -T_{\text{printed}} - 0.005(2 + R)$ ($0.005(2 + R) = 77/6200$ for $q = 4$ and $89/7000$ for $q = 20$). With $\sigma^2 = 17.91$ ($\rho = 0.99$), (v) gives $J - h = 189, 213, 522, 371$ for rows 30, 40, 50, 60: the probability that averages of exact design expectations under the stated model are as printed is at most $2^{-189} \le 10^{-56}$, $2^{-213} \le 10^{-64}$, $2^{-522} \le 10^{-157}$ and $2^{-371} \le 10^{-111}$ respectively, for every $K \ge 1$.
Corrected claim: for each of rows 30, 40, 50 and 60, under the described Gaussian model and the stated rounding tolerance, the probability that both the $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{HT}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}$ means are averages of exact design expectations within $0.005$ of the printed values is at most the corresponding bound in (vi), for every $K\ge1$. These bounds give extremely strong evidence that a computation or its description needs correction; they do not establish deterministic impossibility, identify a faulty column or supply replacement values.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\hat t$, $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$, $A$, Proposition 1: main pp. 233–234; $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)$: main p. 237; $\hat\mu_{HT} \equiv \hat t/N$ and ‘computed exactly using expressions from Propositions 1 and 2’: supplement p. A1; the periodic design, the outcome model and the demeaned outcome: supplement pp. A3–A4; $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{WR}(\hat\mu_{HT})$ with $p_k = \pi_k/m$: supplement p. A3; all in the standing assumptions. The samples $G_g$ and their probabilities: P027-T2 (i). The calibration $\beta^2 = 900\rho^2(N-1)/(16N)$ uses $\sigma_y = 30$ and the divisor-$(N-1)$ standard deviation of the periodic sizes; (iii)–(vi) do not depend on $\beta$. ‘Mean from sims.’ is read as the average over generated populations of exact conditional design expectations; the number of populations $K$ is not stated in the supplement and is not assumed. $\|\cdot\|$ is the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^N$.
canonical_claim.note: P027-N004 is rated an error, Minor: a numerical finding about four rows of a supplementary table. Sol's verdict is confirmed_in_part, evidence type complete_derivation, upheld on re-run; repair cost weaker_conclusion (a numerical and reporting repair, not a theorem repair). It is on the list because the finding is itself a mathematical derivation and the author's instruction asks for a formal statement for every error with mathematical content; there is no corrected table to state, so the target is the formal content of the finding. Parts (i)–(iii) are exact identities for every demeaned population (deterministic); (ii) uses second moments only; (iv)–(vi) are the probabilistic step and hold under independent Gaussian noise: the incompatibility is an explicit probability bound, not a deterministic impossibility. Not established (Sol): which column is wrong, the alleged discrepancy in every row, the low-$\rho$ $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}$ discrepancies, or the floating-point cause conjectured by a reader. The identities of (i) and the ratio $-5/(9q)$ are shared with P027-T2 and P027-T6. The table rows and all constants were checked against the rendered supplement page and recomputed independently when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.location: p. 234 (PDF p. 6), Section 2.2, with its proof and the paragraph that follows it
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed (p. 234): “Proposition 1. When $s^0$ refers to a sample from a design with some $\pi_{kl} = 0$, $$\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)\right] = \mathrm{Var}(\hat t) + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}} y_k y_l = \mathrm{Var}(\hat t) + A.$$”
Printed proof: “The result follows from, $$\mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{k \in s^0}\sum_{l \in s^0}\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U:\pi_{kl} > 0\}} I_k I_l\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}\right]$$ $$= \sum_{k \in U}\mathrm{Var}(I_k)\left(\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\right)^2 + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} > 0\}}\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}$$ $$= \mathrm{Var}(\hat t) + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}} y_k y_l = \mathrm{Var}(\hat t) + A.$$”
The paragraph after the proof (p. 234): “The standard Horvitz-Thompson variance estimator, if applied to designs with zero pairwise inclusion probabilities, can therefore have a positive or a negative bias. If the $y_k, y_l$ values are always nonnegative (or always nonpositive), then the bias is always nonnegative.”
Hypotheses the paper attaches: the standing assumptions (a finite population, fixed outcomes, a sampling design with $\pi_k > 0$ for every $k$: ‘condition 1 holds, as we assume throughout’); $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$ on $s^0$ is the sum over pairs of sampled units, equal to $\sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U:\pi_{kl} > 0\}} I_k I_l\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}$ with $\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l) = \pi_{kl} - \pi_k\pi_l$ and $\pi_{kk} = \pi_k$.
The headline claim (P027-H1) has three parts. (a) The identity $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)] = \mathrm{Var}(\hat t) + A$, where $A = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}} y_k y_l$ is a sum over ordered pairs of distinct units. (The clause ‘with some $\pi_{kl} = 0$’ describes the case of interest; when no pair has $\pi_{kl} = 0$ the sum is empty, $A = 0$, and the identity is the unbiasedness of Section 2.1.) (b) If $y_k \ge 0$ for all $k$, or $y_k \le 0$ for all $k$, then $A \ge 0$, so the bias $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)] - \mathrm{Var}(\hat t)$ is nonnegative. (c) The bias can have either sign: there are designs and outcome vectors with $A > 0$ and others with $A < 0$ (for instance the design of P027-T3 with $y = (1, 1, 1)$, where $A = 4$, and with $y = (1, 1, -1/4)$, where $A = -1$).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $U$, $\pi_k$, $\pi_{kl}$, $I_k$, $\hat t$, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat t)$, $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$, $s^0$ and $A$: pp. 232–234 (PDF pp. 4–6), transcribed in the standing assumptions. $\mathrm{Var}(\hat t) = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in U}\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}$ (p. 233) is the variance of $\hat t = \sum_k I_k y_k/\pi_k$ over the design.
canonical_claim.note: An exact finite-population identity; both readers checked it line by line and by complete enumeration (candidates.json, P027-H1: held up). The examples named in (c) are the validator's for finding P027-N002, not the paper's. The supplement's uses of the proposition are the subject of findings P027-E003 and P027-E004 (P027-T10, P027-T11, P027-T1, P027-T2).

canonical_claim.location: pp. 235–236 (PDF pp. 7–8), Section 3.1, with its proof
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed (p. 235): “Consider the following variance estimator: $$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t) = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U:\pi_{kl} > 0\}} I_k I_l\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l} + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}}\left(I_k\frac{|y_k|^{a_{kl}}}{a_{kl}\pi_k} + I_l\frac{|y_l|^{b_{kl}}}{b_{kl}\pi_l}\right),$$ where $a_{kl}, b_{kl}$ are positive real numbers such that $1/a_{kl} + 1/b_{kl} = 1$ for all pairs $k, l$ with $\pi_{kl} = 0$. The estimator is guaranteed to produce an expected value greater than or equal to the true variance for all designs, and is thus conservative. We state this property formally: Proposition 2. The expected value of $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)$, $$\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)\right] \ge \mathrm{Var}(\hat t).$$”
Printed proof (pp. 235–236): “By Young's inequality, $$\frac{|y_k|^{a_{kl}}}{a_{kl}} + \frac{|y_l|^{b_{kl}}}{b_{kl}} \ge |y_k||y_l|,$$ if $1/a_{kl} + 1/b_{kl} = 1$. Define $A^*$ such that, $$A^* = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}}\frac{|y_k|^{a_{kl}}}{a_{kl}} + \frac{|y_l|^{b_{kl}}}{b_{kl}} \ge \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}}|y_k||y_l| \ge \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}} y_k y_l = A$$ and $$A^* \ge \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}}|y_k||y_l| \ge \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}} -y_k y_l = -A.$$ Therefore $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat t) + A + A^* \ge \mathrm{Var}(\hat t).$$ The associated Horvitz-Thompson estimator of $A^*$ would be $$\hat A^* = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}}\left(I_k\frac{|y_k|^{a_{kl}}}{a_{kl}\pi_k} + I_l\frac{|y_l|^{b_{kl}}}{b_{kl}\pi_l}\right),$$ which is unbiased by $E(I_k) = \pi_k$ and $E(I_l) = \pi_l$. Since $E(\hat A^*) = A^*$, by Proposition 1, $$\mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{k \in s^0}\sum_{l \in s^0}\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l} + \hat A^*\right] = \mathrm{Var}(\hat t) + A + A^*$$ $$\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)\right] \ge \mathrm{Var}(\hat t).$$”
Hypotheses the paper attaches: the standing assumptions ($\pi_k > 0$ for all $k$; fixed real outcomes, of any signs); for every ordered pair $(k, l)$ of distinct units with $\pi_{kl} = 0$, positive real numbers $a_{kl}, b_{kl}$ with $1/a_{kl} + 1/b_{kl} = 1$. In the display for $A^*$ both fractions are summands of the double sum.
The headline claim (P027-H2), with the steps of the proof that carry it: (a) $A^* \ge |A|$, that is $A^* \ge A$ and $A^* \ge -A$; (b) $\mathrm{E}(\hat A^*) = A^*$; (c) $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)] = \mathrm{Var}(\hat t) + A + A^*$; (d) $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)] \ge \mathrm{Var}(\hat t)$, for every design satisfying condition 1 and every outcome vector.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)$, $a_{kl}$, $b_{kl}$, $A^*$, $\hat A^*$: pp. 235–236 (PDF pp. 7–8), transcribed in the statement. $A$, $\hat t$, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat t)$, $I_k$, $\pi_k$, $\pi_{kl}$, $\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)$, Proposition 1: pp. 233–234, standing assumptions and P027-T20. Young's inequality as used: for real $u, v \ge 0$ and $a, b > 1$ with $1/a + 1/b = 1$, $u^a/a + v^b/b \ge uv$ (the paper cites it by name only). The first double sum of $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)$ is $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$ applied to $s^0$; the second is $\hat A^*$.
canonical_claim.note: An exact finite-population inequality; both readers checked the proof and ran exact finite cases (candidates.json, P027-H2: held up; the caveat recorded there is the wrong cross-reference in the proof of Corollary 2, P027-T23, and the paragraph on totalling clusters, P027-T3, P027-T4, P027-T8, on which no proposition depends). Section 4 (p. 239) restates (a) as ‘the fact that $A^* \ge A$’ (headline claim P027-H5, an interpretive remark that is not a separate target).

canonical_claim.location: pp. 236–237 (PDF pp. 8–9), Section 3.1, with its proof
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed (pp. 236–237): “$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)$ is justified as a conservative estimator for the case when $A$ is not known to be positive. This estimator is unbiased under a special condition: Corollary 1. If, for all pairs $k, l$ such that $\pi_{kl} = 0$, (i) $|y_k|^{a_{kl}} = |y_l|^{b_{kl}}$ and (ii) $-y_k y_l = |y_k||y_l|$, $$\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)\right] = \mathrm{Var}(\hat t).$$”
Printed proof (p. 237): “By (i), (ii) and Young's inequality, $$\frac{|y_k|^{a_{kl}}}{a_{kl}} + \frac{|y_l|^{b_{kl}}}{b_{kl}} = |y_k||y_l| = -y_k y_l.$$ Therefore, $$A^* = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}}\frac{|y_k|^{a_{kl}}}{a_{kl}} + \frac{|y_l|^{b_{kl}}}{b_{kl}} = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}}|y_k||y_l| = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}} -y_k y_l = -A.$$ It follows that $\mathrm{Var}(\hat t) + A + A^* = \mathrm{Var}(\hat t)$ and $\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)\right] = \mathrm{Var}(\hat t)$.”
Hypotheses the paper attaches: those of Proposition 2 (the standing assumptions; for every ordered pair $(k, l)$ of distinct units with $\pi_{kl} = 0$, positive reals $a_{kl}, b_{kl}$ with $1/a_{kl} + 1/b_{kl} = 1$), and (i) and (ii) for every such pair. The corollary states sufficient conditions; it does not claim they are necessary.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)$, $a_{kl}$, $b_{kl}$, $A^*$: pp. 235–236, transcribed in P027-T21. $A$, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat t)$, $\pi_{kl}$: pp. 233–234, standing assumptions. The equality case of Young's inequality as used: for $u, v \ge 0$ and $a, b > 1$ with $1/a + 1/b = 1$, $u^a = v^b$ implies $u^a/a + v^b/b = uv$. Condition (ii) says $y_k y_l \le 0$.
canonical_claim.note: An exact finite-population identity; both readers checked the equality case and an exact example (candidates.json, P027-H3: held up; for instance two strata of two units with one unit drawn from each, $y = (3, -3, 5, -5)$ and $a_{kl} = b_{kl} = 2$: $\mathrm{Var}(\hat t) = \mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)] = 136$).

canonical_claim.location: p. 237 (PDF p. 9), Section 3.2, with its one-line proof
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed (p. 237): “In general, it would be difficult to assign optimal values of $a_{kl}$ and $b_{kl}$ for all pairs $k, l$ such that $\pi_{kl} = 0$. Instead, we examine one intuitive case, assigning all $a_{kl} = b_{kl} = 2$: $$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t) = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U:\pi_{kl} > 0\}} I_k I_l\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l} + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}}\left(I_k\frac{y_k^2}{2\pi_k} + I_l\frac{y_l^2}{2\pi_l}\right).$$ As a special case of $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)$, $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)$ is also conservative: Corollary 2. The expected value of $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)$, $$\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)\right] \ge \mathrm{Var}(\hat t).$$”
Printed proof: “For all pairs $k, l$ such that $\pi_{kl} = 0$, $1/a_{kl} + 1/b_{kl} = 1$. Proposition 1 therefore holds.”
Hypotheses the paper attaches: the standing assumptions only ($\pi_k > 0$ for all $k$; fixed real outcomes of any signs); the estimator is $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)$ with $a_{kl} = b_{kl} = 2$ for every pair with $\pi_{kl} = 0$.
The proof as printed cites Proposition 1; the result it applies is Proposition 2 (finding P027-E006 (a); Sol's repair: “Proposition 2 therefore applies.”): since $1/2 + 1/2 = 1$, Proposition 2 gives the inequality.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)$: p. 237, transcribed in the statement. $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)$ and Proposition 2: pp. 235–236, P027-T21. $\mathrm{Var}(\hat t)$, $I_k$, $\pi_k$, $\pi_{kl}$, $\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)$: p. 233, standing assumptions.
canonical_claim.note: An exact finite-population inequality; held up as a mathematical statement by both readers (candidates.json, P027-H4). The wrong cross-reference in its proof is part (a) of finding P027-E006 (Minor; a misprint, not a target of its own). Not printed, but used by the validators: with $a_{kl} = b_{kl} = 2$, $A^* = \sum_k\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}}(y_k^2 + y_l^2)/2$ and the bias is $A + A^* = \tfrac12\sum_k\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}}(y_k + y_l)^2 \ge 0$.
